parts.title: Arranging work experience
parts.context: A student phones a company about his work experience placement.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a student phoning a company about a work experience placement. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Brightside Design, Mrs Chambers speaking.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Hello. My name's Daniel, and I'm calling about my work experience placement with your company. I'm in Year Eleven.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Yes, I've been expecting your call. I'll just check a few details with you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller is in Year Eleven, so 'Eleven' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Could you give me your surname, please?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: It's Mortimer. That's M-O-R-T-I-M-E-R.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Thank you, Daniel. And which school are you from?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Greenfield High School.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Your placement is for two weeks, isn't it?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Yes, starting on Monday the ninth of June.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: And what interests you about our company?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: I'd like to work in graphic design. I've been teaching myself to use design software at home.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: That's good to know. You'll start at nine o'clock on the first day. Later in the week, the start is half past eight, but not on the first day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: What should I wear? I don't have a suit.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: You don't need one, but please wear smart clothes. No jeans or trainers, because clients sometimes visit the office.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Where should I go when I arrive?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Come to reception, and ask for me. I'll take you to meet your supervisor, who'll show you round the building.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: What about lunch? Should I bring something?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: There's a canteen on the ground floor, where the food is cheap and rather good, so you needn't bring anything unless you prefer to.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Who will be my supervisor?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Mr Okafor, that's O-K-A-F-O-R, one of our senior designers. He's looking forward to meeting you.

script.speaker: chambers
script.text: Is there anything I need to do for school?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Yes, you need to keep a diary of what you do each day, and your teacher will ask to see it afterwards. It's easiest to write it up in the last half hour of each day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A new bus station
parts.context: A council officer explains the layout of a new bus station.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a council officer presenting plans for a new bus station at a public meeting. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm David Hughes, and I'm the project manager for the new Central Bus Station. Let me show you the layout. Please look at the plan. The main entrance is at the bottom, and it opens onto the concourse in the middle.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: At the top on the left, you'll find the ticket office, where passengers can buy tickets and get information. Next to it, at the top in the middle, is a large waiting hall, with seats and screens showing departure times. The bus bays are at the top on the right.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: On the left side of the concourse are the toilets, and on the right side is the café, which will have a lot of windows, so that passengers can see the buses arriving. We're hoping a well-known company will run it.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: At the bottom on the left, we've planned a secure bike park, because many commuters cycle to the station. And at the bottom on the right is the taxi rank, close to the entrance, so that people with luggage don't have to walk far.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Now, some questions I'm often asked. When will the station open? The building work will take about eighteen months, so you'll see it in use in the autumn of the year after next.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: What will happen to the buses in the meantime? They will use temporary stops on Park Street, which is two minutes' walk from the old station. We'll put up signs, and our staff will be there to help.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: The new station will have twelve bus bays, which is four more than the old one, so there will be space for new routes, and for the larger buses that we're ordering.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: On the roof, we'll install solar panels, which will provide most of the electricity for the building. It's part of the council's plan to be carbon neutral.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: You can see the full plans on the council's website, and also in the library, where a model of the station is on display. We'd really like to hear your comments. Now, who has the first question?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Preparing for a debate
parts.context: Two politics students prepare for a debate on the voting age.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two politics students, Hira and Sean, preparing for a debate on the voting age. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: Sean, we need to prepare for the debate on Thursday. Remind me of the motion.

script.speaker: sean
script.text: 'This house believes that the voting age should be lowered to sixteen.' And we're proposing it, which means we argue in favour.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: How did we end up on that side?

script.speaker: sean
script.text: We drew lots, and we were lucky. I think it's the easier side, though our tutor says the other team will have some strong arguments.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: What will their strongest argument be?

script.speaker: sean
script.text: Maturity. They'll say that sixteen-year-olds aren't mature enough to make important decisions. We'll need a good answer.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: How long does each speaker have?

script.speaker: sean
script.text: Five minutes for the main speeches, and two for the replies, so we need to be concise.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: Let me describe how the debate works. First, each team gives an opening statement, setting out its main points.

script.speaker: sean
script.text: Then we support our points with evidence. We have some polls and studies from countries that have already lowered the voting age.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: The other team is allowed to ask a question, and we must answer it straight away, without notes.

script.speaker: sean
script.text: After that, each side gives a rebuttal, where we respond to what our opponents have said.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: And at the end, the chair asks the audience to vote, and the team that changes the most minds wins.

script.speaker: sean
script.text: Right, I'll write the opening statement tonight, and you can find the evidence.

script.speaker: hira
script.text: Fine. Shall we practise on Wednesday?

script.speaker: sean
script.text: Yes, in the common room at six.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: penguins
parts.context: A biology lecture on how penguins survive.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about penguins. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Penguins are among the most popular animals in the world, yet they live in some of the harshest places on Earth. Today I'd like to explain how they survive.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: There are about eighteen species of penguin, and all of them live in the Southern Hemisphere, mainly in Antarctica, on sub-Antarctic islands, and along the coasts of South America, Africa and Australia. None lives in the Arctic.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. Instead, they are superb swimmers. Their wings have become stiff flippers, which they use to move through the water, at speeds of more than thirty kilometres an hour for the fastest species.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Staying warm in icy water is a challenge. A penguin has a thick layer of fat, and very dense feathers, which are waterproofed with oil from a gland near the tail. The bird spreads the oil over its feathers every day.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The emperor penguin, the largest species, has the most extraordinary life cycle. It breeds in the middle of the Antarctic winter, when temperatures fall far below freezing. The female lays a single egg, and the male balances it on his feet, under a flap of skin, for about two months, without eating anything at all.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Meanwhile, the females walk to the sea to feed, and return when the chick hatches. To survive the freezing winds, the males stand close together in a huddle, taking turns to move to the warmer centre.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Penguins feed mainly on krill, which are small shrimp-like animals, as well as fish and squid. They have to watch out for predators such as leopard seals.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The biggest threat to penguins today is the loss of sea ice, caused by climate change, since many species depend on it for breeding and for their food supply. Next week we'll look at polar bears.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
